lines.text: Wine tasting is a structured method of evaluating wine using sight, smell, and taste — transforming casual drinking into informed appreciation. The process follows a systematic approach taught by wine educators worldwide. First, examine the wine's appearance: hold the glass against a white background and observe the colour, clarity, and intensity. A young white wine is pale lemon; with age, it deepens to gold. A young red shows purple-ruby tones; an aged red shifts toward garnet and brick. Next, assess the nose: swirl the glass to release volatile aromatics, then inhale. Primary aromas come from the grape itself (fruit, floral, herbal); secondary aromas from fermentation (yeast, brioche); tertiary aromas from ageing (vanilla, leather, earth). Finally, taste: take a small sip, drawing air across the wine to amplify flavours. Assess sweetness, acidity, tannin (in reds), alcohol, body, and flavour intensity. The finish — how long flavours linger after swallowing — indicates quality; a long, complex finish suggests a superior wine. Professional tasters spit rather than swallow to remain objective across multiple wines. Wine vocabulary can seem pretentious to outsiders, but it serves a practical purpose: precise descriptors help professionals communicate consistently about flavour, quality, and style across languages and cultures.
